sentences.text: Galeamopus is an extinct diplodocid sauropod dinosaur known for having a weak skull.
The name Galeamopus means "helmet need" in Latin, referring to the fragile braincase of the type specimen.
The genus name is a pun on the first names of discoverers William Utterback and William Holland, translating to "want helmet".
The genus name is derived from the Latin term galeam, the accusative of galea, meaning "helmet", and opus, meaning "need".
The name also alludes to the fact that the small neurocranium of the holotype needs coverage.
Researchers identified six unique anatomical traits specific to the species Galeamopus hayi.
The genus is defined by thirteen unique anatomical features, which researchers deemed enough to justify its separation from other dinosaurs.
The thirteen unique traits found in Galeamopus represent the exact minimum number used in the study to separate different genera.
In Galeamopus, the ulna is at least 76% as long as the humerus.
The underside joint surface of the radius is angled at approximately 15 degrees relative to the shaft.
The top surface of the shinbone (tibia) features a pinched process behind the cnemial crest.
The first fossil specimen attributed to Galeamopus was collected by Marshall P. Felch in September 1884 at Garden Park, Colorado.
The type specimen of Galeamopus was discovered by William H. Utterback in 1902 near Sheridan, Wyoming.
The genus was identified from a partial skeleton discovered by William H. Utterback in 1902 near Sheridan, Wyoming.
In 1906, William Jacob Holland referred the skeleton to Diplodocus when he described the neurocranium.
Holland classified the specimen as a new species of Diplodocus, Diplodocus hayi, in 1924.
In 2015, Emanuel Tschopp, Octávio Mateus, and Roger Benson renamed this species as a separate genus, Galeamopus.
The genus Galeamopus was established by Tschopp and colleagues in 2015.
Emanuel Tschopp, Octávio Mateus, and Roger Benson renamed the genus Galeamopus in 2015.
The genus holotype is HMNS 175, previously CM 662, the original skeleton.
In 2017, the specimen nicknamed "Max" was designated the type specimen for the second species, Galeamopus pabsti.
In 2017, the specimen "Max" was designated as the type specimen for a second species of Galeamopus, G. pabsti, by Tschopp and Mateus.
The species Galeamopus pabsti was named in honor of Swiss paleontologist Dr. Ben Pabst.
Galeamopus is classified in the class Saurischia.
Galeamopus belongs to the family Diplodocidae.
The parent group of Galeamopus is Diplodocinae.
Galeamopus is considered an advanced sauropod placed as a member of the family Diplodocidae, within a clade alongside Diplodocus in the subfamily Diplodocinae.
Galeamopus lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 155 million years ago, in the lower Morrison Formation of Wyoming.
Galeamopus lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages, between 154.8 and 143.1 million years ago.
The holotype was found in a layer of the lower zone of the Morrison Formation dating to the Kimmeridgian.
